finding_key: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts::the cli login url — which carries the whole nonce + pkce challenge pair — is handed to `open()`, i.e. placed in a child process's argv, where any local user can read it and defeat all three new loopback bindings
evidence: Verified in packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts: `openBrowser` passes the full start URL (nonce + code_challenge) to `open(url)`, which spawns `xdg-open`/`open` with the URL in argv, readable by other local users — undercutting the deliberate effort in `announceLoginUrl` to keep that URL out of stderr/logs. The replay chain also holds against the code shown: a local attacker reusing the URL gets their own `browserBinding` cookie in `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` (so that binding does not stop them), `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` mints a code carrying the copied challenge and echoes the victim's nonce, `nonceMatches` in login.ts passes, and `CliAuthStore.consumeCode` accepts the victim's verifier since it hashes to the copied challenge — victim's CLI ends up holding the attacker's tokens. I rate it minor rather than higher because the exploit window is ~30s (listener lifetime), requires a hostile local co-tenant, and any browser launch inherently exposes the URL in some process's argv (the `open` Windows path may even use stdin), so the real error is the docs' claim that the cookie binding closes the shared-host case.
